A 125 cc automatic scooter on Koh Samui costs about 150–350 THB a day, a 150–160 cc model 250–450 THB, and a month 2,000–4,500 THB. You legally need your home licence plus an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category; without it you can be fined and your travel insurance is unlikely to pay out after a crash. The helmet fine has been up to 2,000 THB per person since 1 June 2025, and you should never leave your passport as a deposit.

Good to know: prices were last checked on 1 November 2026 and vary by shop, season and bike condition. Laws and fines quoted here are for general information; they are not legal advice.

Licence and IDP rules

To ride legally as a tourist in Thailand you need:

  • your full national driving licence with the motorcycle (category A) entitlement, and
  • an International Driving Permit (IDP) issued in your home country, also showing the motorcycle category.

Thailand recognises IDPs under both the 1949 Geneva Convention and the 1968 Vienna Convention. The UK government tells British visitors to carry the 1968 IDP with their UK licence, and you cannot buy an IDP once you are abroad. A car-only (category B) licence does not cover a scooter, even a 110 cc one. Licences from ASEAN countries (Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia) are accepted without an IDP under the ASEAN agreement.

Do you have the right licence?

  • Home licence with motorcycle (A) + IDP with motorcycle stamped: yes, you can ride legally.
  • Home licence with motorcycle (A), but no IDP: not legal; expect a fine at checkpoints and insurance problems.
  • Car-only licence, with or without IDP: not legal on any scooter.
  • No licence: not legal. Use Grab, taxis, songthaews or tours with pickup.
  • ASEAN national licence with motorcycle category: accepted.

Riding without a valid licence or IDP is typically fined 500–1,000 THB. The bigger cost comes after a crash, when insurers refuse claims for medical bills that can reach hundreds of thousands of baht.

The helmet law and fines

Helmets are compulsory for the rider and every passenger, on every road, including short hops to the 7-Eleven. Since 1 June 2025 the fine has been up to 2,000 THB per person, up from the older 500–1,000 THB levels, and police enforce it far more consistently than the licence rules. If both rider and passenger are without helmets, the total can reach 4,000 THB. Any figure of "500 THB" you see online is out of date.

  • Fasten the chin strap; an unfastened helmet counts as no helmet in a crash.
  • Rental helmets are often thin shells. For a long stay, buy a proper certified helmet from a bike shop or mall on the island.
  • Children must wear a helmet that fits; adult helmets on small heads do not protect them.

Deposits and passports

Shops ask for a deposit to cover damage and theft. Typical amounts are 1,000–3,000 THB cash for a 125 cc scooter and 3,000–5,000 THB for a 150–160 cc bike. Some shops, often near the piers, still ask for your original passport. Do not hand it over: the UK Foreign Office advises against leaving your passport as a guarantee with motorbike or jet-ski rental businesses, because companies may keep it against claimed damage. Offer a cash deposit and a photocopy instead. Get a written receipt that shows the deposit amount, the bike's registration and the return date.

Insurance: rental vs travel policy

  • Compulsory insurance: every Thai-registered vehicle must carry basic compulsory motor insurance, which covers limited medical costs for injured people. It does not cover damage to the bike or your liability for other vehicles.
  • Shop insurance: some shops sell extra cover for damage or theft with an excess. Read what is excluded (often tyres, mirrors and falls).
  • Unregistered bikes: the UK Foreign Office warns that many rental scooters in tourist areas are unregistered and cannot legally be used on a public road. Check that the bike has a number plate and a current tax disc, and ask to see the registration book.
  • Travel insurance: most policies cover scooter riding only if you hold the right licence at home, carry the IDP, wear a helmet and stay within the engine size limit (often 125 cc). Many exclude riding after drinking.
  • Off-island: rental contracts almost always void cover if the bike leaves Samui, including on a ferry to Koh Phangan.

Compare policies on our Koh Samui travel insurance page.

Checklist before you ride

  1. Walk around the bike and photograph and video every panel, the mirrors, the seat and the exhaust, with the shop owner present. Make sure the timestamp is on.
  2. Check both brakes stop the bike firmly.
  3. Check tyre tread and pressure; bald tyres are lethal on wet roads.
  4. Test the headlight, brake light, indicators and horn.
  5. Check the number plate, tax disc and registration book (or a copy).
  6. Note the fuel level and the mileage.
  7. Try the helmet on and fasten it; ask for another if it is loose or cracked.
  8. Agree the return time and the late fee in writing.
  9. Save the shop's phone number and ask what to do in a breakdown.

Where to rent, by area

Rental shops line the main roads of Chaweng, Lamai, Bophut, Maenam and Nathon, and almost every hotel desk can arrange a bike. Independent shops are cheaper; established shops with many bikes and a fixed address are easier to deal with if something goes wrong. Ask for a written contract in English, read the damage and theft clauses, and check what happens if the bike breaks down. For long stays, monthly rentals in Maenam, Nathon and Lipa Noi are the best value. We don't recommend or link individual rental shops.

Riding on Samui

Samui's 51 km ring road (Route 4169) is mostly two lanes with fast traffic, trucks and constant turning traffic. The worst risks for visitors are:

  • Hills: Route 4170 in the south-west and many villa access roads are steep concrete with tight bends. Use the rear brake and engine braking on descents to avoid overheating the brakes, and walk the bike down anything you are unsure of.
  • Rain: the first minutes of rain lift oil from the road. From October to December, flooded dips hide potholes.
  • Sand and gravel on bends, especially near beaches and building sites.
  • Dogs that run into the road, especially at night.
  • Turning traffic: cars and pickups often pull out or turn across your path without looking; scooters overtake on both sides. Ride defensively and keep a gap.
  • Night riding: many roads are poorly lit; other riders often have no lights.
  • Drink: the drink-drive limit is 0.05% blood alcohol, and 0.02% for riders under 20 or without a full licence. Many crashes involve alcohol.

Thailand has one of the highest road death rates in the world, and most victims are on motorcycles. If you do not ride at home, Samui is not the place to learn. Read our Koh Samui roads guide before you set off.

Police checkpoints

Checkpoints are regular near Chaweng Lake Road, near the airport and along the ring road. Officers check helmets, licences and IDPs, and issue a ticket you pay at the police station or on the spot against a receipt. Carry your licence, IDP and a copy of your passport, and stay polite and calm at every check.

Damage disputes and scams

Damage disputes are the most common rental complaint. Shops may claim for scratches that were already there, typically 800–2,000 THB for a scratched panel and 500–1,500 THB for a mirror.

  • Your timestamped photos and video from the start of the rental are your best evidence.
  • Do not agree to a price on the spot if you think the claim is false. Ask to see the damage list and compare it with your photos.
  • If the dispute escalates or you feel threatened, call the Tourist Police on 1155 (English-speaking).
  • Never let a shop keep your passport.

More on common tricks is in our Koh Samui scams guide and on the Tourist Police page.

If you crash

  • Call 1669 for an ambulance and 191 or 1155 for the police.
  • Take photos of the scene, the vehicles and the other party's plate.
  • Get a police report: your insurer will need it.
  • Contact your travel insurer's emergency line before major treatment if you can.
  • Don't sign documents you cannot read; ask the Tourist Police for help.

Private hospitals are listed on our Koh Samui hospitals page.

Fuel, parking and security

  • Fuel: a 125 cc scooter tank holds only a few litres, enough for one or two loops of the island. Fill up at petrol stations on the ring road; roadside bottles of fuel cost more and are sometimes diluted.
  • Parking: park in marked scooter bays where they exist, never on yellow-and-white or red-and-white kerbs, and never inside the Fisherman's Village walking street on Friday evenings, where bikes are towed and cost 500 THB or more to release.
  • Theft: always lock the steering and take the key. Many rentals include a chain lock; use it overnight. Thefts are reported to the police for insurance, and a stolen bike usually costs you the deposit plus its value unless you have theft cover.
  • Belongings: do not leave bags in the front basket at traffic lights; snatch thefts happen in Chaweng.

Riding with a passenger or children

A loaded scooter brakes later and leans differently, which catches out many visitors on Samui's hills. Ride slower than you would alone, let the passenger mount only when you are ready, and make sure they keep their legs away from the exhaust: exhaust burns on the inner calf are so common on the islands that locals call them the "Thai tattoo". Children must sit behind the rider, hold on with both hands and wear a helmet that fits. Never carry more than one passenger, and never ride with a child in front of you.

Long-term rental tips

  • Monthly rates in Maenam, Nathon and Lipa Noi are the lowest on the island; ask for a newer bike and a service before you take it.
  • Agree in writing who pays for routine maintenance such as oil changes, tyres and brake pads. On most monthly deals, the shop pays for wear and you pay for damage.
  • Check the tax disc expiry date; if it runs out during your rental, the shop must renew it.
  • If you stay longer than your IDP allows, or on a long-stay visa, consider a Thai driving licence. Our long-stay guide explains the process.

Returning the bike

Return the bike with the same fuel level, at the agreed time and in daylight if possible, so you and the shop can inspect it together. Have your photos from the start ready. Collect your full deposit before you hand back the key, and do not leave the deposit "to be transferred later". If you are leaving the island early in the morning, agree a drop-off arrangement the day before.

Alternatives to a scooter

  • Grab and taxis: Grab short hops cost about 80–120 THB in Chaweng, Bophut and Lamai; see getting around Koh Samui.
  • Songthaews: 30–80 THB along the ring road by day.
  • A driver for the day: about 2,000–3,000 THB per car.
  • A car: safer in the rain and better for families; see car rental.
  • Tours with pickup: our boat tours include hotel pickup from most areas of Koh Samui, such as the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult). For the island's hills and viewpoints without riding yourself, see the jungle safari; for off-road fun on a guided track, try an ATV quad bike session.
